headline: Medium-risk pair: Airflow can orchestrate Chatwoot actions, creating default-path data leakage and cascading-error exposure; no direct prompt-injection channel is documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared channel or direct output ingestion is documented. Airflow has broad network egress and can call APIs, while Chatwoot exposes integrations such as Slack/Dialogflow/Shopify/Linear, so a manual or integration bridge could carry attacker-controlled text. This is plausible but not default and the blast radius is limited without a proven parser bridge.
conditions: IF Airflow task output is copied into a Chatwoot integration payload
IF Chatwoot parses Airflow-produced text as instructions
mitigations: Disable any copy-paste bridge between Airflow logs and Chatwoot inputs
Require explicit allowlists for integration payload fields
Strip markup and instruction-like text from Airflow outputs
Use a human review step before posting to Chatwoot
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all cross-system messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, interaction history, orders, messages, and reports, while Airflow has broad network egress and API access. If Airflow workflows move those records into external services or logs, leakage can occur in default configurations. Airflow itself is not shown handling secrets, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Airflow DAGs ingest Chatwoot customer records
IF those records are sent from Airflow to any external API or log sink
mitigations: Restrict Airflow tasks to minimum necessary fields
Mask customer identifiers in task logs
Block outbound calls except approved endpoints
Review DAGs for any export of Chatwoot data
requires-engineering: add DLP controls on Airflow egress

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write to external mutable systems through APIs/integrations, and Airflow has broad network egress. Chatwoot’s integrations imply overlapping write paths to third-party services, so concurrent updates can conflict even without filesystem overlap. The profiles do not show locking or coordination, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF Airflow and Chatwoot write to the same external resource
IF no external locking or idempotency key is configured
mitigations: Assign one system as the writer of record
Add idempotency keys to outbound actions
Serialize writes through a queue
Check for duplicate updates in logs
requires-engineering: implement resource-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Airflow can generate automated outputs and Chatwoot can act on customer-support workflows and integrations. If Chatwoot treats Airflow-produced data as authoritative, an upstream mistake can cascade into incorrect customer actions or reports. No verification step is documented, so the interaction is plausible in default use but not proven high-impact.
conditions: IF Chatwoot consumes Airflow-generated reports or tickets
IF Chatwoot acts on those inputs without human verification
mitigations: Add a validation step before Chatwoot actions
Require human approval for automated customer-facing changes
Compare Airflow outputs against source records
Flag low-confidence records for review
requires-engineering: add schema validation between systems

E_compliance.rationale: Chatwoot explicitly touches customer data and related records, while Airflow can move data across networked systems. If Airflow processes the same customer data under different retention or residency rules, compliance mismatches can arise. The profiles do not document certifications or residency, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Airflow processes customer data subject to retention or residency rules
IF Airflow exports that data to a system with different policy controls
mitigations: Inventory the data classes flowing through Airflow
Align retention settings across both systems
Restrict cross-border transfers
Document the lawful basis for each transfer
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement to pipelines
